summary:
Beacon is a web app and mobile prototype that turns NASA satellite fire data into early warnings, focused on Yakutia (Sakha Republic), Russia's largest fire region, where satellites are often the only eyes on the forest. It combines 25 years of MODIS and VIIRS fire detections (14.4
  million for Yakutia since 2000) into one continuous record, shows live fires on a 3D globe updated every hour, and uses a machine-learning model, trained on fire history and NASA weather data, to rank every 28 km square of Sakha by its chance of fire in the coming week. In tests
  on years it never saw, its riskiest 10% of squares contained 76% of the following week's fires in 2021 and 80% in 2026, so people and responders can see where danger is building before the fire reaches them.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

  Beacon turns NASA satellite fire detections into early warnings for places where satellites are often the only eyes, starting with Yakutia (Sakha Republic), Russia's largest fire region.

  - Collecting the data: it gathers every fire detection from NASA FIRMS: MODIS since 2000, and VIIRS since 2012 from the S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 satellites. That's 14.4 million detections for Yakutia alone. It removes low-confidence detections, gas flares and industrial heat, and

    stores everything in one database.

  - One record across sensors: because MODIS and VIIRS see fires differently, Beacon calibrates the older MODIS counts against VIIRS, square by square. This gives one continuous record from 2000 to today that keeps working after MODIS retires.

  - Live view and history: a 3D globe shows the last 7 days of fires, updated every hour, and a burn calendar shows month-by-month fire activity for any area.

  - Prediction: for Yakutia, a machine-learning model reads recent fires, neighbouring fires, 25 years of history and NASA POWER weather. It ranks every 28 km square by its chance of fire in the next 7 days.

  - Results on years it never saw: its riskiest 10% of squares contained 76% of the following week's fires in 2021 and 80% in 2026.

  

  What benefits does it have?

  - Warning time: a week before a square first caught fire in 2021, it was already on the watch list (the riskiest 20% of Sakha) 6 times out of 10. That's time to prepare villages and send crews.

  - No break in the record: the harmonized record means long-term fire trends don't break as MODIS retires and S-NPP stops (it did on 2 November 2026).

  - Free and open: all data sources are free, and the code is open.

  

  What is the intended impact?

  In Yakutia, two-thirds of the forest is legally allowed to burn unwatched, and in 2021 only 9% of fires were put out on the first day. Beacon aims to give residents, local authorities and responders an early, honest view of where danger is building, so the next village gets warned

  before the fire reaches it. The same approach can extend to any fire region on Earth.

  What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  - Website: TypeScript with Next.js and React, Three.js for the 3D globe, Leaflet for maps.

  - API: Python with FastAPI, SQLAlchemy and PostgreSQL. 

  - Model: pandas, NumPy, SciPy and scikit-learn (gradient boosting, plus logistic regression as a comparison).

  - Running it: Docker containers on standard laptops; no special hardware.

  - Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS), NASA POWER weather, NASA GIBS imagery, Open-Meteo forecasts, geoBoundaries borders.

  - Code: stored on GitHub. 

  

  How is the project creative?

  - One continuous record: instead of treating MODIS and VIIRS as separate datasets, we built a single record that outlives either sensor.

  - A watch list, not a single guess: instead of claiming to predict exactly where the next fire starts, Beacon makes a ranked daily watch list, which is a format responders can act on.

  - The brand: the lighthouse logo (a beacon over the world's fires) turns its light while the data loads.

  

  What factors did our team consider?

  - Honest testing: the model is tested on years and areas it never saw, and compared against simple rules. We also report where it's weak: brand-new fires, mostly lit by lightning.

  - False alarms: we filter out gas flares, mines and oil fields.

  - Satellite limits: cloud and smoke can hide fires, and some satellites are retiring.

  - Data that changes: satellite data and fire seasons change from year to year.

  - Accessibility: the animation respects reduced-motion settings. 

  - Not official: Beacon isn't an official warning service and isn't affiliated with NASA.
